title: Cascode Frequency Response
intro: The cascode was invented for speed: the CG device on top holds the drain of the input device nearly still, so $C_{GD1}$ is barely Miller-multiplied, while the input keeps the high impedance of a CS stage.

blocks.alt: Cascode: Vin drives node A (gate of M1) through RS; CGS1 from A to ground and CGD1 from A to node X. M1's drain is node X, which has capacitance CX to ground and is the source of M2. M2's gate is at Vb; its drain is the output node Y with capacitance CY to ground and RD to VDD.
blocks.caption: Three nodes, three poles.

blocks.text: The gain from A to X is about $-g_{m1}/(g_{m2} + g_{mb2})$, roughly $-1$ for similar devices, so $C_{GD1}$ is multiplied by about 2 instead of $1 + g_m R_D$:

blocks.tex: \omega_{p,X} = \frac{g_{m2} + g_{mb2}}{2C_{GD1} + C_{DB1} + C_{SB2} + C_{GS2}}, \qquad \omega_{p,Y} = \frac{1}{R_D(C_{DB2} + C_L + C_{GD2})}

blocks.text: $\omega_{p,X}$ is about half of $\omega_T$ of M2 once the extra capacitances are counted, usually well above the other two. Which of A and Y dominates depends on $R_S$ and the load.

With a current-source (or cascode) load, the resistance looking up into M2's source is large at DC, which would suggest a low pole at X and a large Miller factor for $C_{GD1}$. In practice the transfer function hardly changes. Modelling M1 as a current $I_{in}$ into X and an ideal load:

blocks.tex: \frac{V_{out}}{I_{in}} = -\frac{g_{m2}r_{o2} + 1}{C_X s}\cdot\frac{1}{1 + (1 + g_{m2}r_{o2})\frac{C_Y}{C_X} + C_Y r_{o2}s} \approx -\frac{g_{m2}}{C_X s}\cdot\frac{1}{\frac{C_Y}{C_X}g_{m2} + C_Y s}

blocks.text: so $V_{out}/V_{in} \approx -\frac{g_{m1}g_{m2}}{C_X C_Y s}\cdot\frac{1}{g_{m2}/C_X + s}$ and the pole at X is still $g_{m2}/C_X$. By the time frequencies approach that pole, $C_Y$ has shorted the output and the high resistance at X is gone. The same argument keeps the Miller factor of $C_{GD1}$ near 2 when $C_L$ is large.
Cascode current source at high frequency
Looking into the drain of M2 with $Z_X = r_{o1} \parallel (1/C_X s)$:
The output impedance has a pole at $1/(r_{o1}C_X)$, which is low because $r_{o1}$ is large; above it the high output impedance (and the gain it provides) fades.

blocks.title: Cascode against CS
blocks.text: $R_S = 2\text{ k}\Omega$, $C_{GS1} = 100\text{ fF}$, $C_{GD1} = 20\text{ fF}$, $g_{m1} = g_{m2} = 4\text{ mS}$ (ignore $g_{mb}$), $C_{DB1} = C_{SB2} = 30\text{ fF}$, $C_{GS2} = 100\text{ fF}$, $R_D = 5\text{ k}\Omega$, total output capacitance 150 fF. Find the three poles, and the input pole of a plain CS stage with the same gain $g_m R_D = 20$.
blocks.answer: Cascode: 568 MHz, 3.18 GHz, 212 MHz. CS input pole: 153 MHz.

blocks.text: In a cascode current source $r_{o1} = 20\text{ k}\Omega$ and $C_X = 100\text{ fF}$. Above what frequency does $Z_{out}$ start to fall?
